claims.statement: For a fixed trained GP posterior with differentiable scalar mean m(x) and twice-differentiable latent variance v(x), take a prescribed Gaussian test input X~N(mu,Sigma) independent of the posterior function conditional on the training data and fixed hyperparameters. The source expands m to first order and v to second order about mu. Integrating these truncated expressions gives the predictive mean approximation m(mu) and latent variance approximation v(mu)+0.5*tr(H_v(mu)*Sigma)+grad(m)(mu)^T*Sigma*grad(m)(mu). This combines the expected conditional variance and the variance of the linearized conditional mean. A Gaussian with these moments is an additional approximation to the predictive law, provided the resulting variance is valid.

For iterative autoregressive prediction the report carries a full Gaussian covariance of the lagged outputs. The local expansion gives Cov(X,f(X)) approximately Sigma*grad(m)(mu), with the transpose used for Cov(f(X),X). This cross-covariance forms the new row and column while the retained lag block shifts forward. If predicting a future noisy output rather than the latent function value, add its independent observation-noise variance once to the new output diagonal. Training noise already used in the GP posterior and this future output noise play different roles. Using only independent lag variances is a different approximation.

evidence.locator: Sections 4.1–4.2, PDF pp. 11–13; Equations 32–35 and the lag covariance matrix, PDF p. 13

claims.statement: A second-order Taylor expansion of the conditional variance is not a general assertion of second-order accuracy for the predictive moments: the source retains only a first-order expansion of the conditional mean. A curator unit-kernel example conditioned on the exact observation f(0)=1 and X~N(0,s) gives Taylor mean 1 and Taylor variance s, whereas exact integration gives mean 1/sqrt(1+s) and variance s/(1+s). The mean error is of order s as s approaches zero, even though the posterior-mean gradient vanishes at the expansion point. At Sigma=0 the formulas reduce to ordinary fixed-input GP prediction.

evidence.locator: Section 3.1, exact squared-exponential integrals, Equations 10–13, PDF p. 4

claims.statement: The local Taylor variance is not guaranteed nonnegative for arbitrary input uncertainty. A curator calculation for a unit-amplitude, unit-lengthscale squared-exponential GP conditioned on an exact f(0)=0, with input mean 1 and variance 2, gives Taylor variance 1-3/e<0 while the exact integrated variance is 1-exp(-1/5)/sqrt(5)>0. This deliberately nonlocal case limits an unrestricted covariance claim; it is not an empirical reproduction or a refutation of a justified small-uncertainty approximation. An invalid computed covariance cannot be interpreted as a Gaussian predictive distribution without a separately justified correction.

The local Taylor procedure is distinct from analytic squared-exponential Gaussian-input moment integration, which the technical report lists as future work and the proceedings paper presents separately. Moreover, propagating a Gaussian lag covariance while repeatedly treating the current input as independent of the uncertain function does not preserve all dependence created by one shared dynamics function across a trajectory. The later correlation-aware trajectory approaches address that different approximation; this record does not identify them with the earlier local Taylor method.

limitations: The method is a local approximation requiring sufficient smoothness and input uncertainty small enough for the retained expansions to be useful. Gaussian test-input independence, fixed training locations/data and fixed hyperparameters are explicit assumptions; uncertain training locations and hyperparameter integration are not solved here.

The first-order mean omits the curvature term 0.5*tr(H_m*Sigma). The scalar negative-variance example also prevents a universal positive-semidefinite covariance claim. No general error bound, calibration guarantee or automatic covariance-repair procedure is asserted.

The technical report changes its squared-exponential width notation: early widths are lengthscales in a denominator, while Equation 25 uses inverse squared lengthscales. Any implementation must choose one consistent parameterization. The record uses posterior derivatives directly and does not copy incompatible width symbols across sections.

Full lag covariance handles correlation between uncertain regressor components, but does not retain the complete shared-function trajectory dependence. Gaussian closure also omits higher moments. A local covariance formula is not exact nonlinear trajectory propagation.

The source forecasting mean can coincide with a mean-only rollout because this particular mean approximation is m(mu); the covariance correction changes the uncertainty estimate. Source comparisons on synthetic dynamics and pH data do not establish universal accuracy, superiority or calibrated coverage, and their numerical results are not curated here.

The exact-observation unit-kernel examples are curator analytic checks, not fitted-model or benchmark reproductions. No author implementation, training, paid provider or stochastic simulation was run. The record remains DRAFT after author self-review.

temporal_dependence_reading.title: On Simulation and Trajectory Prediction with Gaussian Process Dynamics
temporal_dependence_reading.page_numbering: PDF and printed indices1–11; official PMLR metadata120:424–434,2020; no conversion of printed indices into article page labels is assumed.
temporal_dependence_reading.abstract_interpretation: The paper identifies an independence assumption in established iterative GP prediction and proposes conditional trajectory sampling, finite-feature function sampling and correlation-aware linearization. Its demonstrations are scoped illustrations, not a universal error bound.
method_notes: PDF1–2 explicitly cites Girard2003 moment propagation among methods implicitly assuming successive function evaluations independent. Persistent latent-function uncertainty induces dependence; ignoring it can underestimate trajectory uncertainty, not a guaranteed inequality for all nonlinear systems.

PDF2–3 contrasts persistent and freshly redrawn Gaussian offset or gain with the same one-step marginals. Figure1 uses linear or squared-exponential kernels and20000trajectories. The locally calculated noiseless f(x)=A*x example is a curator linear-kernel illustration, not source replication.

PDF4 describes vector GP dynamics plus independent additive Gaussian process noise. The implicit trajectory Gaussian expression has state-dependent random kernel locations and is not a general assertion that the nonlinear trajectory law is Gaussian.

PDF5–6 sequential trajectory sampling conditions each next GP prediction on this sampled trajectory’s prior transition pairs, with the specified process-noise covariance. Incremental Cholesky retains prior draws. Exactness is under the specified GP/dynamics model, not a statement about real-world dynamics.

PDF6 finite-feature function sampling samples Gaussian coefficients once per trajectory, preserving that approximate function through rollout. Finite bases approximate the kernel except special finite-rank cases; fixed-basis rollout cost differs from basis construction and fitting.

PDF6–7 linearizes the mean and freezes joint kernel blocks along the deterministic mean trajectory. The covariance A(K+I tensor Q)A^T retains cross-time GP covariance. Noncommuting Jacobian product order and advertised quadratic cost require implementation-specific audit before asserting them as generic results.

PDF8 reports simple prior examples, no training-data benchmark here. A near-origin uncertain-gain example defeats accurate linearization even though correlation is retained. There is no global accuracy guarantee.

PDF9–11 all references read. New full-method leads include Deisenroth–Huber–Hanebeck2009 analytic GP filtering, Lázaro-Gredilla et al.2010 sparse-spectrum GP regression, Pan et al.2017 uncertain sparse-spectrum prediction, and Ialongo et al.2019 recurrent-GP mean-field corrections. They require identity and primary-method checks.

notes: PDF1–2 identifies GP-ADF: Gaussian assumed-density filtering with GP transition and measurement functions. Dynamics x_k=f(x_{k-1})+w and y_k=g(x_k)+v use additive white Gaussian noise with diagonal stated covariance. PDF3 Section4 fixed GP posterior and Section4.1 Gaussian-input exact moments. Equations8–10 use ambiguous p(E[h(x)]|...) notation; the intended predictive mixture is not a distribution over an already deterministic expectation. Fixed hyperparameters and trained functions; exact first two moments under specified Gaussian input do not make its full law Gaussian.

PDF4 Section4.2 trains conditionally independent GP output components at common input locations. Outputs become correlated through a shared uncertain input; product-of-conditional-means cross moments give off-diagonal covariance. PDF5 Section5.2 additionally replaces joint (state,measurement) by a Gaussian with computed cross covariance, then applies the standard Gaussian conditioning mean and covariance equations14. PDF5 Section5.3 explicitly lists two Gaussian approximations.
